summary:
Iraq is among the most dangerous countries in the world for a trans visitor. On 27 April 2024 the Council of Representatives passed an amendment to the 1988 Law on Combatting Prostitution that explicitly criminalises consensual same-sex relations, gender-affirming healthcare and diverse gender expression. The President signed the legislation on 29 June 2024 and it has been in force since 1 July 2024. The Library of Congress Global Legal Monitor, Human Rights Watch and ILGA Asia all record it as the operative legal baseline.

The penalties are severe. Consensual same-sex relations carry 10 to 15 years' imprisonment. Undergoing or performing a gender-affirming procedure carries 1 to 3 years, applied to both the transgender person and the doctor, which places transition itself beyond the law; court-ordered procedures on intersex people are excluded. Country coverage also records penalties of up to 15 years together with fines and deportation, so removal from the country is a stated consequence. Broadcast reporting adds penalties for 'promoting homosexuality', an offence with no settled definition in the sources.

Legal gender recognition does not exist. Iraq has no framework for changing legal sex markers, and the 2024 amendment's criminalisation of what it calls biological sex changes based on personal desires and inclination effectively closes off any route to recognised documentation. Marriage is restricted to a man and a woman under Article 3 of the Iraqi Personal Status Law 1959 and Article 1 of the Iraqi Kurdistan Personal Status Law 1992, with Article 7 requiring couples to produce medical documents certifying they are not infected with AIDS. A 1981 amendment to the Personal Status Law allows a wife to divorce a husband found guilty of a homosexual relationship, treated as infidelity.

Violence against gender-nonconforming people is documented and largely unpunished. A BBC investigation found dozens, possibly hundreds, of gay people killed in recent years while authorities turned a blind eye, with the UN stating that state neglect makes Iraq a perpetrator. In October 2023 a prominent Iraqi TikToker was fatally shot in Baghdad amid a crackdown on the LGBTQ community. The US State Department's 2012 Human Rights Report already documented societal discrimination and violence based on perceived sexual orientation and gender identity alongside torture and impunity. Supporters of the 2024 law framed it as upholding religious values; rights groups condemned it and Human Rights Watch has called for its repeal.

Practical protection is thin. The UK Home Office's July 2025 country-of-origin information assessment finds risk from both state and hybrid actors and non-state actors, and treats internal relocation and certification as material questions for LGBT+ asylum claims. A visitor should expect no official remedy for anti-trans violence and no lawful basis for their gender-affirming care or presentation.
tangentialFactors:
Attacks have historically targeted gender expression as much as sexuality. In early 2012 a wave of killings struck 'emo' teenagers accused of homosexuality on the basis of their clothing, carried out by Shi'a death squads of the Mahdi Army; flyers circulated in Baghdad naming individuals and threatening them unless they cut their hair and abandoned nonconformist dress. The pattern links visible nonconformity, not only disclosed relationships, to lethal risk.

The hostility has an official as well as a social dimension. Broadcast coverage of the 2024 amendment recorded supporters presenting it as upholding religious values, and the legislation passed with parliamentary majorities rather than under executive decree. International bodies have responded with documented objections: Human Rights Watch called for repeal within weeks of passage, the UN characterised state neglect of anti-LGBT killings as complicity, and the UK Home Office produced a dedicated country-of-origin information document on sexual orientation and gender identity risk in July 2025.

Historical precedent exists for punitive state treatment of stigmatised health conditions. After AIDS reached Iraq in 1986, Saddam Hussein ordered all Iraqis with the disease relocated to a special prison facility, an episode that bears on how the state links health status to confinement and that informs the medical screening language still present in the marriage law.
localsOnly:
Protection machinery for Iraqi LGBT people is run overwhelmingly by civil society rather than the state. Iraqi LGBT, established in September 2005, works on relocating LGBTQ people to safer countries, provides legal help for asylum seekers and maintains safe houses inside Iraq. The International Railroad for Queer Refugees, founded in 2008, supplies financial and resettlement assistance to LGBTQ asylum seekers fleeing persecution on sexual orientation or gender identity grounds.

OWFI led more than 40 local organisations in campaigning to change Iraq's Anti-Shelter Policy, which had permitted only government-run shelters to operate. Rasan expanded its project work from 2016 as a partner of COC Nederland in the Pride Program, known locally as Crossing Iraqi Rainbow. Iraqueer, formed in March 2015, runs education work including published guides on security and health safety, video material and workshops on gender and sexuality, and provides advocacy and safety support in crisis.

Asylum and internal relocation are therefore handled largely by these organisations, and the UK Home Office assessment addresses internal relocation and certification as open questions rather than settled protections. No domestic legal aid scheme, no hate-crime statute covering gender identity, and no official complaint route for anti-trans violence appear in the sources.
outOfScopeNotes:
Two sourcing discrepancies remain unresolved. The amendment date is given as 27 April 2024 by Human Rights Watch and as 28 April 2024 by ILGA Asia; the sources do not reconcile the difference. Penalty reporting is also inconsistent: the 10 to 15 year range for consensual same-sex relations and 1 to 3 years for gender-affirming procedures are broadly consistent, but country coverage separately states up to 15 years with fines and deportation without specifying which offence that ceiling applies to.

No source in the inventory addresses entry and border formalities for trans visitors. There is nothing on visa application gender markers, passport presentation, airport or land-border screening, or whether secondary inspection risks disclosure. Enforcement practice since 1 July 2024 is likewise unsourced: the inventory documents the law, its penalties and a pattern of societal violence, but contains no prosecution figures, arrest data or court decisions under the amendment.

Detention conditions for trans detainees, access to hormone therapy or continuing care while in Iraq, and the availability of safe accommodation for short-stay visitors are not covered by any listed source. The country-of-origin information document addresses asylum claimants rather than travellers, and its risk findings are drawn from a different evidentiary standard than visitor guidance.
